Qwen.content:
# Alibaba Cloud (Qwen)

Alibaba Cloud's DashScope API provides OpenAI-compatible access to Qwen language models. Use OpenAI provider options supported by your chosen model.

## Setup

To use Alibaba Cloud's API, set theDASHSCOPE_API_KEY environment variable or specify via apiKey in the configuration file:
export DASHSCOPE_API_KEY=your_api_key_here

## Configuration

The provider uses OpenAI provider options; support varies by model. Example:
providers:
  - alibaba:qwen3.8-max # Simple usage
  - id: alibaba:qwen3.7-plus # Aliases: alicloud:, aliyun:, dashscope:
    config:
      temperature: 0.7
      apiKey: your_api_key_here # Alternative to DASHSCOPE_API_KEY environment variable
      apiBaseUrl: https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1 # Optional: Override default API base URL

note

The equivalent provider prefixes arealicloud:, aliyun:, and dashscope:. For new configurations, Alibaba recommends qwen3.7-plus for balanced use, qwen3.8-flash for lower cost, or qwen3.8-max for stronger reasoning. Check the model catalog for your region; model availability differs by region.

If you're using the Alibaba Cloud Beijing region console, switch the base URL tohttps://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1 instead of the international endpoint.

## Supported Models

The built-in Alibaba provider implements OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and text embeddings. The catalog below also lists separate realtime, speech recognition, and image generation services. Listing a model here does not add those endpoints to this provider. Choose a model supported by your selected endpoint and region.

### Qwen 3 Flagship

- qwen3.8-max / qwen3.8-max-0902 - Current flagship with text, image, and video input and a 1M-token context window
- qwen3.8-flash - Faster Qwen3.8 model with a 1M-token context window
- qwen3.7-plus / qwen3.7-plus-2026-05-26 - General-purpose model with thinking, vision, and tool calling
- qwen3.7-flash / qwen3.7-flash-2026-07-15 - Lower-cost Qwen3.7 model
- qwen3.7-max / qwen3.7-max-2026-06-08 - Previous flagship
- qwen3.6-plus / qwen3.6-flash and qwen3.5-plus / qwen3.5-flash - Previous model families
- qwen3-max - Supports reasoning and tool calling
- qwen3-max-preview - Preview version with thinking mode support
- qwen3-max-2025-09-23 - September 2025 snapshot
- qwen-max - 32K context (30,720 in, 8,192 out)
- qwen-max-latest - Always updated to latest version
- qwen-max-2025-01-25 - January 2025 snapshot
- qwen-plus / qwen-plus-latest - 128K-1M context (thinking & non-thinking modes)
- qwen-plus-2025-09-11, qwen-plus-2025-07-28, qwen-plus-2025-07-14, qwen-plus-2025-04-28, qwen-plus-2025-01-25 - Dated snapshots
- qwen-flash / qwen-flash-2025-07-28 - Latency-optimized general model
- qwen-turbo / qwen-turbo-latest / qwen-turbo-2025-04-28 / qwen-turbo-2024-11-01 - Earlier low-latency model; see qwen-flash
- qwen-long-latest / qwen-long-2025-01-25 - 10M context for long-text analysis, summarization, and extraction

### Qwen 3 Omni & Realtime

- qwen3.8-omni-flash - Text output from text, image, audio, and video input through Chat Completions; use the separate realtime API for qwen3.8-omni-flash-realtime
- qwen3-omni-flash / qwen3-omni-flash-2025-09-15 - Supports speech and vision in thinking and non-thinking modes
- qwen3-omni-flash-realtime / qwen3-omni-flash-realtime-2025-09-15 - Streaming realtime with audio stream input and VAD
- qwen3-omni-30b-a3b-captioner - Dedicated audio captioning model (speech, ambient sounds, music)
- qwen2.5-omni-7b - Qwen2.5-based multimodal model with text, image, speech, and video inputs

### Reasoning & Research

- qwq-plus - Alibaba's reasoning model (commercial)
- qwq-32b - Open-source QwQ reasoning model trained on Qwen2.5
- qwq-32b-preview - Experimental QwQ research model (2024)
- qwen-deep-research - Long-form research assistant with web search
- qvq-max / qvq-max-latest / qvq-max-2025-03-25 - Visual reasoning models (commercial)
- qvq-72b-preview - Experimental visual reasoning research model
- DeepSeek models (hosted by Alibaba Cloud):
- deepseek-v4.1-flash / deepseek-v4-pro-0813 - Current hosted Flash and Pro models; these IDs differ from the direct DeepSeek API
- deepseek-v3.2-exp / deepseek-v3.1 / deepseek-v3 - DeepSeek V3 models
- deepseek-r1 / deepseek-r1-0528 - DeepSeek reasoning models
- deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-{1.5b,7b,14b,32b} - Distilled on Qwen2.5
- deepseek-r1-distill-llama-{8b,70b} - Distilled on Llama

### Vision & Multimodal

Commercial:

- qwen3-vl-plus / qwen3-vl-plus-2025-09-23 - High-res image support with long context (thinking & non-thinking modes)
- qwen3-vl-flash / qwen3-vl-flash-2025-10-15 - Fast vision model with thinking mode support
- qwen-vl-max - 7.5K context, 1,280 tokens/image
- qwen-vl-plus - High-res image support
- qwen-vl-ocr - OCR-optimized for documents, tables, handwriting (30+ languages)

Open-source:

- qwen3-vl-235b-a22b-thinking / qwen3-vl-235b-a22b-instruct - 235B parameter Qwen3-VL
- qwen3-vl-32b-thinking / qwen3-vl-32b-instruct - 32B parameter Qwen3-VL
- qwen3-vl-30b-a3b-thinking / qwen3-vl-30b-a3b-instruct - 30B parameter Qwen3-VL
- qwen3-vl-8b-thinking / qwen3-vl-8b-instruct - 8B parameter Qwen3-VL
- qwen2.5-vl-{72b,7b,3b}-instruct - Qwen 2.5 VL series

### Audio & Speech

- qwen3-asr-flash / qwen3-asr-flash-2025-09-08 - Multilingual speech recognition (11 languages, Chinese dialects)
- qwen3-asr-flash-realtime / qwen3-asr-flash-realtime-2025-10-27 - Real-time speech recognition with automatic language detection
- qwen3-omni-flash-realtime - Supports speech streaming with VAD

### Coding & Math

Commercial:

- qwen3-coder-plus / qwen3-coder-plus-2025-09-23 / qwen3-coder-plus-2025-07-22 - Coding agents with tool calling
- qwen3-coder-flash / qwen3-coder-flash-2025-07-28 - Fast code generation
- qwen-math-plus / qwen-math-plus-latest / qwen-math-plus-2024-09-19 / qwen-math-plus-2024-08-16 - Math problem solving
- qwen-math-turbo / qwen-math-turbo-latest / qwen-math-turbo-2024-09-19 - Fast math reasoning
- qwen-mt-{plus,turbo} - Machine translation (92 languages)
- qwen-doc-turbo - Document mining and structured extraction

Open-source:

- qwen3-coder-480b-a35b-instruct / qwen3-coder-30b-a3b-instruct - Open-source Qwen3 coder models
- qwen2.5-math-{72b,7b,1.5b}-instruct - Math-focused models with CoT/PoT/TIR reasoning

### Qwen 2.5 Series

All support 131K context (129,024 in, 8,192 out)

- qwen2.5-{72b,32b,14b,7b}-instruct
- qwen2.5-{7b,14b}-instruct-1m

### Qwen 2 Series

- qwen2-72b-instruct - 131K context
- qwen2-57b-a14b-instruct - 65K context
- qwen2-7b-instruct - 131K context

### Qwen 1.5 Series

8K context (6K in, 2K out)

- qwen1.5-{110b,72b,32b,14b,7b}-chat

### Qwen 3 Open-source Models

Open-source Qwen3 models with thinking mode support:

- qwen3-next-80b-a3b-thinking / qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct - Next-gen 80B (September 2025)
- qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507 / qwen3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507 - 235B July 2025 versions
- qwen3-30b-a3b-thinking-2507 / qwen3-30b-a3b-instruct-2507 - 30B July 2025 versions
- qwen3-235b-a22b - 235B with dual-mode support (thinking/non-thinking)
- qwen3-32b - 32B dual-mode model
- qwen3-30b-a3b - 30B dual-mode model
- qwen3-14b, qwen3-8b, qwen3-4b - Smaller dual-mode models
- qwen3-1.7b, qwen3-0.6b - Edge/mobile models

### Third-party Models

Kimi (Moonshot AI):

- kimi-k3 - Current Kimi model
- kimi-k2.6 - Previous Kimi model with a 256K context window
- moonshot-kimi-k2-instruct - First open-source trillion-parameter MoE model in China (activates 32B parameters)

Z.AI (GLM):ZHIPU/GLM-5.3 and glm-5.2. Check the regional model catalog for access and endpoint requirements.

### Embeddings

Usealibaba:embedding:<model> for embeddings. The alibaba:<model> shorthand sends chat requests.

- text-embedding-v3 - 1,024d vectors, 8,192 token limit, 50+ languages
- text-embedding-v4 - Latest Qwen3-Embedding with flexible dimensions (64-2048d), 100+ languages
- qwen3.7-text-embedding - Newer Qwen3.7 text embeddings; availability depends on the region

defaultTest:
  options:
    provider:
      embedding:
        id: alibaba:embedding:text-embedding-v4

### Image Generation

Thealibaba provider does not call image-generation endpoints. To use models such as qwen-image-plus, configure the HTTP provider for Alibaba's image API.

See the DashScope model catalog for availability.

## Additional Configuration

Put DashScope-specific request fields underconfig.passthrough. For example, enable_thinking controls thinking mode on Qwen3.8 and Qwen3.7 chat models:
providers:
  - id: alibaba:qwen3.8-max
    config:
      passthrough:
        enable_thinking: true

Standard OpenAI parameters (temperature, max_tokens) are supported. Base URL:https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1 (or https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1 for the Beijing region).

For API usage details, see Alibaba Cloud documentation.

## 阿里Qwen4-Max发布 AI模型竞争升级 云业务弹性增强

 | 时间：2026年11月15日 19:41:31 中财网 

CFi.CN讯：数据显示，阿里于11月11日开放Qwen4-Max-Preview大模型预览版，支持文本、图片、视频多模态输入及百万Token上下文，具备深度思考、联网搜索、工具调用等能力，聚焦编程开发、办公协同与复杂智能体任务。同期，Anthropic、Google、百度、MiniMax密集发布新一代AI模型，API价格下探，推理效率提升，行业技术迭代明显加速。
近期机构研报指出，大模型从‘参数竞赛’转向‘场景落地+成本优化’双驱动，阿里云作为国内最大公有云厂商，Qwen系列快速迭代将强化其政企客户AI解决方案的交付能力与定价话语权。研报认为，模型能力升级有望带动云业务ARPU值提升，尤其在金融、政务、制造等高价值行业渗透加速。

Kimi.description: Moonshot (Kimi) Moonshot AI provides an OpenAI-compatible API for its Kimi models — the Kimi K3 and K2 thinking models and the Moonshot v1 generation models. ... - Kimi K3 — flagship thinking model, 1M context ... - Kimi K2 — thinking models, 256k context...
Kimi.content:
# Moonshot (Kimi)

Moonshot AI provides an OpenAI-compatible API for its Kimi models — the Kimi K3 and K2 thinking models and the Moonshot v1 generation models. The Moonshot provider extends the OpenAI provider, so all of its options are supported.

## Setup

- Get an API key from the Kimi (Moonshot) platform.
- Set theMOONSHOT_API_KEY environment variable or specify apiKey in your config.

Kimi K3 requires a successful account top-up of at least $1; see the access requirements.
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3

Bothmoonshot:<model> and moonshot:chat:<model> resolve to the chat completions endpoint. If you omit the model, the provider defaults to kimi-k3.

## Available Models

Moonshot's lineup rotates over time — call the list models API (GET https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/models) for the live set. As of writing:

- Kimi K3 — flagship thinking model, 1M context:kimi-k3 (released July 2026). Always-on reasoning, native image and video understanding, and a top-level reasoning_effort control (see below).
- Kimi K2 — thinking models, 256k context:kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.5, kimi-k2.7-code, kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed. These reason before answering and emit a separate reasoning stream (see below).
- Moonshot v1 — legacy generation models:moonshot-v1-8k, moonshot-v1-32k, moonshot-v1-128k (context-length variants) and the vision variants moonshot-v1-8k-vision-preview / moonshot-v1-32k-vision-preview / moonshot-v1-128k-vision-preview; existing accounts may also see the auto-router moonshot-v1-auto in the list-models API. The moonshot-v1 series and kimi-k2.5 are closed to newly registered users and sunset platform-wide on August 31, 2026.

The olderkimi-k2-0711-preview, kimi-k2-0905-preview, kimi-k2-turbo-preview, kimi-k2-thinking, kimi-k2-thinking-turbo, and kimi-latest ids were discontinued in 2026 — Moonshot recommends migrating to kimi-k3.

## Configuration
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3 # flagship thinking model — leave sampling params unset
  - id: moonshot:moonshot-v1-8k # legacy generation model — accepts arbitrary sampling
    config:
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 1024

### Configuration Options

The provider accepts every option the OpenAI provider supports. Commonly used:

- temperature, max_tokens, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty
- stream
- response_format (JSON mode), tools / tool_choice (function calling)
- showThinking — set to false to drop a thinking model's reasoning from the graded output (default true)
- cost, inputCost, outputCost, cacheReadCost — Moonshot ships no built-in price table, so set these to track cost. Every override is in USD per token. Moonshot's official pricing page publishes rates in USD per 1 million tokens, so divide each published rate by 1,000,000 before configuring it. inputCost/outputCost take precedence over the flat cost; cacheReadCost prices cached prompt tokens.

For example, these illustrative per-million rates convert to per-token overrides. Check the official pricing page for the current rates for your model before using them.
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
    config:
      inputCost: 0.000003 # $3.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      cacheReadCost: 0.0000003 # $0.30 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      outputCost: 0.000015 # $15.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k2.6
    config:
      inputCost: 0.00000095 # $0.95 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      cacheReadCost: 0.00000016 # $0.16 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      outputCost: 0.000004 # $4.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000

Any other parameter supported by the OpenAI provider is forwarded as-is.

## Kimi thinking models

Thekimi-k3 and kimi-k2.x models are reasoning models and behave differently from the moonshot-v1 family:

- Fixed sampling parameters. Kimi pinstemperature (1.0 with thinking on), top_p, n, and the penalties to fixed values and returns a 400 ("invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model") for any other value. The provider therefore does not send promptfoo's default temperature/max_tokens for kimi-* models — leave them unset (recommended) or set temperature: 1. The moonshot-v1 models accept arbitrary sampling values.
- Reasoning output. Kimi returns a separatereasoning_content stream that promptfoo surfaces with a Thinking: … prefix. Set showThinking: false when you assert on structured output (for example is-json) so the reasoning doesn't contaminate the parsed result.
- Token budget. Reasoning tokens count against the output budget. When you leave the token limit unset the provider lets Moonshot apply its server default (32k for K2.x, 131k for K3); if you set one, leave generous headroom for the answer. Moonshot's canonical field ismax_completion_tokens (max_tokens is a deprecated alias) — the provider sends max_completion_tokens for kimi-* models whichever of the two you configure.
- Controlling thinking. The two generations use different, mutually exclusive controls:
- kimi-k3 is always thinking and accepts a top-level reasoning_effort field, which the provider forwards from config.reasoning_effort. Supported values are low, high, and max (the default). Do not send the K2.x thinking parameter to K3 — the API rejects it.
- kimi-k2.6 and kimi-k2.5 support thinking: { type: disabled } (pass it via config.passthrough); kimi-k2.7-code is always thinking. The thinking parameter is K2.x-only.
- Settingconfig.reasoning_effort on a non-K3 model is a configuration error and the provider fails fast with a clear message instead of sending it.

providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
    config:
      showThinking: false
      reasoning_effort: max # optional: low, high, or max (default)
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k2.6
    config:
      passthrough:
        thinking: { type: disabled } # K2.x only: turn reasoning off

See the Kimi K3 quickstart and Using Thinking Models for the full behavior matrix.

## Vision

The vision models (moonshot-v1-*-vision-preview) and the multimodal Kimi models (kimi-k3, kimi-k2.5, kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.7-code, kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed) accept base64-encoded image input using the standard OpenAI image_url content format. Moonshot does not accept remote image URLs — embed images as data: URIs or reference files uploaded to the Kimi platform as ms://<file-id>. Video input is supported by kimi-k3, kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.7-code, and kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed, referenced the same way after uploading via the files API. See Use the Kimi Vision Model.

## Example Usage
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
  - id: openai:gpt-4o-mini

prompts:
  - 'Summarize the following in one sentence: {{text}}'

tests:
  - vars:
      text: 'Promptfoo is an open-source tool for testing and evaluating LLM apps.'

A runnable comparison lives in examples/provider-moonshot.

## API Details

- Base URL:https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 (global). China-mainland keys use https://api.moonshot.cn/v1 — point at it with apiBaseUrl, since the global and China platforms issue region-locked keys.
- OpenAI-compatible chat completions API.
- Full API documentation.

## See Also

- OpenAI Provider — compatible configuration options
- Kimi model list and pricing

xAI.content:
# xAI

xAI serves its Grok models through an OpenAI-compatible API that you can add to LibreChat as a custom endpoint.

## Get an API key

Create a key from the xAI console. Add it to your.env file:
XAI_API_KEY=your-api-key

## Configuration

Add the endpoint to thecustom list under endpoints in your librechat.yaml. If your file already has an endpoints.custom list, paste only the - name: entry into it, keeping the same indentation:
endpoints:
  custom:
    - name: "xai"
      apiKey: "${XAI_API_KEY}"
      baseURL: "https://api.x.ai/v1"
      models:
        default: ["grok-beta"]
        fetch: false
      titleConvo: true
      titleMethod: "completion"
      titleModel: "grok-beta"
      modelDisplayLabel: "Grok"

## Notes

- titleMethod: "completion" generates conversation titles through the chat completions endpoint, which is what Grok supports.

cross_cutting.title: Ornith-1.0-9B (agentic coding, text decoder) — Core AI
cross_cutting.description: (MIT, released 2026-06-25) — DeepReinforce's Ornith 1.0 family trains the model to jointly solve coding tasks AND construct the orchestration scaffold that guides the solution...
cross_cutting.content:
# Ornith-1.0-9B (agentic coding, text decoder) — Core AI

The zoo's first agentic-coding / self-scaffolding model. Source:deepreinforce-ai/Ornith-1.0-9B
(MIT, released 2026-06-25) — DeepReinforce's Ornith 1.0 family trains the model to
jointly solve coding tasks AND construct the orchestration scaffold that guides the
solution; the 9B dense is its phone-/Mac-class member (the 397B MoE sibling matches
frontier assistants on SWE-Bench Verified). An image-text-to-text checkpoint; this
card is the text decoder.

Architecturally it is a Qwen3.5 hybrid decoder (model_type qwen3_5) — the same
family as the shipped 0.8B / 2B / Qwen3.6-27B — so it rides the
pipelined engine with zero new export code
(the stock script + --hf-id):

- 32 layers on the 3:1 interleave of GatedDeltaNet linear-attention mixers and gated full attention (full_attention_interval 4 → 8 full / 24 linear);
- full attention: head_dim 256, GQA 16 query / 4 KV heads, partial mRoPE θ=1e7 (text-only positions ≡ plain RoPE), sigmoid output gate;
- linear (GatedDeltaNet): 32 value heads over 16 key heads (the 0.8B/2B/35B GVA ratio), key/value head_dim 128, short causal conv (k=4) + delta rule;
- denseMLP(12288), hidden 4096, untied 248320-vocab lm_head (at the
checkpoint root — the loader's untied branch, like the 27B);
- the checkpoint carries a vision tower (model.visual.*, 333 tensors) and an MTP
config stub but no MTP weights; the text-decoder load skips vision cleanly.

⬇️ Converted.aimodel bundle: ornith_1_0_9b_decode_int8hu_block32_sym/
(9.8 GB, full LanguageBundle incl. tokenizer + chat template; decode-only loop-free,
max_ctx 8192). HF upload user-gated.

## Numbers (verified 2026-07-03)

check | result 
---|---
oracle (fp32 HF eager, margin-validated prompt) | sweep min top-2 margin 0.205 (most 2–8) 
fp16 eager teacher-forced (baseline) | 24/24 exact (16 sweep + 8 decode) 
int8hu eager (ship recipe) | 24/24 exact — zero flips, even at the 0.205 / 0.058-margin knife edges 
engine path (release llm-runner, greedy, raw prompt ids) | 12/12 token-exact ≡ fp32 oracle (int8hu AND int4lin) 
Mac bench int8hu (M4 Max, p128 g256 n3, COREAI_CHUNK_THRESHOLD=1) | decode 48.3 / prefill 48.5 tok/s (trials ±0.1) 
Mac bench int4lin (same rig) | decode 58.9 / prefill 59.0 tok/s (+22%, 7.5 GB) 

Ship recipe = the family ship shape: linear int8 per-block-32symmetric_with_clipping
body (embed/conv/norms fp16) + absmax symmetric per-block-32 int8 on the untied
big-vocab head (clipping crushes outlier head rows — see the knowledge page). Effective
per-token read ≈ 7.7 GB → the 48 tok/s is bandwidth-bound and healthy.

Chat path: the bundled Qwen chat template works as-is (llm-runner --prompt wraps it;
fluent assistant-style code analysis).

## int4 — the family's first clean PTQ pass

int4lin (linear per-block-32, head fp16) gates 24/24 exact on the same eager
teacher-forced rig — including the 0.205 / 0.058-margin knife edges — and the engine
bundle reproduces the oracle greedy 12/12. That is a first for the Qwen3.5 family:
0.8B failed int4 at every scheme, the 2B failed linear per-block-32, the 27B was
borderline (one confident flip). Quantization sensitivity is a model property; this
RL-trained 9B tolerates 4-bit where its siblings don't. Measured: 7.5 GB bundle,
58.9 tok/s decode on M4 Max (+22% over int8hu) — this shape is in the
gemma4/LFM "+~24%" class, not the qwen-2B flat class.

Why int8hu is still the default ship: every instrument we ran is clean for int4, but they are all short-context (48 gated tokens). The gemma4-VL port showed int4 clipping error can compound invisibly until real context lengths (272-token gate caught flips a 27-token gate missed). Until a long-context gate says otherwise, int8hu carries the quality claim; int4lin is one flag away and fully verified at short range.

## iPhone status

int8 at 9.8 GB exceeds the entitled jetsam ceiling (~6.4 GB on iPhone 17 Pro) — Mac ship for v1. int4lin (7.5 GB measured) helps but not enough as-is. The arithmetic route to the phone is int4 body + int8 head (≈ 6.5 GB, at the jetsam edge) or additionally an in-graph int8 embed table (≈ 5.5 GB, real headroom) — both future work, the latter needs the gemma4---tbl-style int8 embed gather.

## Convert it yourself
cd coreai-models && .venv/bin/python \
    ../coreai-models-community/conversion/export_qwen3_5_decode_pipelined.py \
    int8hu --head-sym --hf-id deepreinforce-ai/Ornith-1.0-9B --max-ctx 8192
# gate (eager, fp32-oracle margin rule):
#   _smoke/gen_ornith9b_ref.py (oracle) + _smoke/test_ornith9b_eager_gate.py
COREAI_CHUNK_THRESHOLD=1 llm-benchmark \
    --model exports/ornith_1_0_9b_decode_int8hu_block32_sym -p 128 -g 256 -n 3

Requires the qwen3_5 model overlay + the pipelined-engine extra-states patch (apps/coreai-pipelined-extra-states.patch) — identical requirements to the shipped
qwen3.5 family; nothing new.

## License

Model weights MIT (upstreamdeepreinforce-ai/Ornith-1.0-9B). This conversion keeps
the upstream license; see the HF card for the Ornith 1.0 technical report.

cross_cutting.description: LFM2.5-2.6B — Apple Core AI (.aimodel) LiquidAI's LFM2.5-2.6B converted to Apple's Core AI (the Core ML successor announced at WWDC26), ready to run on iOS 27 / macOS 27.
cross_cutting.content:
# LFM2.5-2.6B — Apple Core AI (.aimodel)

LiquidAI's LFM2.5-2.6B converted to Apple's Core AI (the Core ML successor announced at WWDC26), ready to run on iOS 27 / macOS 27. Same conv + full-attention hybrid as the 1.2B, scaled to 30 layers = 22 short-conv mixers + 8 GQA attention layers, hidden 2048, MLP 10 752, 32 q / 8 kv heads, vocab 128 000. No recurrent scan anywhere, so the decode graph is loop-free by construction and rides Apple'scoreai-pipelined GPU engine with one fixed-shape conv state and no custom
kernels.

This is a reasoning model — the chat template ends the generation prompt with an open<think>, and generations spend their first few hundred tokens thinking. Budget max-tokens
accordingly; a 200-token cap regularly ends mid-thought.

Requires the iOS 27 / macOS 27 beta (Core AI ships with the OS). Conversion code, gates and
knowledge base: coreai-model-zoo.

## Bundles

path | size | prompt tok/s | decode tok/s | oracle gate 
---|---|---|---|---
gpu-pipelined/lfm2_5_2_6b_decode_int8hu_block32_sym | 3.4 GB | 139.5 | 116.7 | PASS 16/16 
gpu-pipelined/lfm2_5_2_6b_decode_int4lin | 2.0 GB | 170.6 | 139.2 | PASS 16/16 

M4 Max, macOS 27.0 (26A5378n), Xcode 27.0 (27A5218g),coreai-torch 0.4.1,
llm-benchmark -p 128 -g 256 -n 3, COREAI_CHUNK_THRESHOLD=1. The gate compares the exported
bundle's greedy decode token-for-token against the fp32 eager oracle; transcripts are in the
zoo card directory.

No iPhone numbers are published here because none were measured.

int8hu is the quality ship. The head is 128 000 × 2048 = 262 M parameters, so leaving it fp16
costs 524 MB of reads per token; untying and quantizing it to int8 buys +8.6 % decode over
plain int8lin (the 1.2B saw +9.3 % for the same reason). The bundle gets bigger — 3.2 → 3.4 GB
— because untying stores an fp16 embedding and an int8 head instead of one shared table. That is
the trade working, not a regression. int8lin is not published: slower than int8hu and only
0.2 GB smaller, so it has no case of its own.

int4lin did not hit the int4 quality cliff, which is worth saying because this family usually
does. Beyond the 16/16 gate, four long greedy generations were read in full — an algorithmic
explanation, iterative Fibonacci with complexity analysis, a clock-arithmetic word problem and a
Japanese instruction — with grammar intact, arithmetic correct and code correct. Four prompts are
not a benchmark: read this as no cliff observed, not int4 is free.

If you are sizing for a phone, note that 524 MB of the 2.0 GBint4lin bundle is the still-fp16
embedding. The remaining size lever on this model is the embedding, not the layers.

## Run it
git clone https://github.com/apple/coreai-models   # + the zoo's engine patches, see below
swift build -c release --product llm-runner

COREAI_CHUNK_THRESHOLD=1 .build/release/llm-runner \
  --model gpu-pipelined/lfm2_5_2_6b_decode_int8hu_block32_sym \
  --prompt "Explain why a hash table lookup is O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case." \
  --max-tokens 512 --sampling-strategy greedy \
  --inference-engine-variant coreai-pipelined --warmup off

--warmup off matters: default warmup submits a synthetic 256-token prefill, and these bundles
are static-S=1, so it fails with a shape-substitution error before generating anything. The
coreai-pipelined-extra-states patch (which carries the conv state) is in the zoo under apps/.

## Converting this family yourself

Two config traps in this checkpoint generation, both silent — nothing raises, and a bundle built without the fix looks like it worked:

- RoPE theta moved. These are transformers-v5-era configs carryingrope_parameters: {rope_theta: 1e7} instead of a flat rope_theta. Read only the flat key and
you fall back to the 1.2B's 1e6 and mis-rotate every position, with no error.
- The tokenizer class does not exist yet.tokenizer_config.json declares
tokenizer_class: "TokenizersBackend", which a transformers-4.x AutoTokenizer cannot resolve.
The chat template also lives in its own chat_template.jinja in this era, so the obvious
workaround ships a bundle with no template. Load tokenizer.json directly and carry the
template across.

Both are handled inconversion/export_lfm2_decode_pipelined.py.

# Models

Core AI is Apple's on-device ML runtime in iOS 27 / macOS 27 and the successor to Core ML: PyTorch models are exported with Apple'scoreai-torch (LLMs: coreai.llm.export) into .aimodel bundles that run on the GPU or the Neural Engine, e.g. Qwen3-8B 4-bit decodes at 94 tok/s on an M4 Max GPU, MLX 90 under the same protocol (apple-silicon-llm-bench, macOS 27 beta 26A5353q, 2026-06-11).

Converted models + conversion recipes for Apple Core AI (.aimodel, iOS 27 / macOS 27):
every model here is downloadable, gated against the original model before it ships, and carries
the recipe that produced it in models/<model>/recipe.toml — rerun it
(zoo_convert.py run <name>), check the published bundle against its source model
(zoo_verify.py), or adapt it for your own port. Don't take the gates on faith — they are run
here, and everything needed to re-run them is published. Each card states what was measured on
which hardware (iPhone tier is device-measured; the large models are Mac-only and say so) and how
strong that model's parity proof is, because it differs per model.
Where the shipped configuration could not be recovered from the repository, the recipe says so
rather than guessing. Model ports are open to everyone — the catalog serves
community ports from the contributor's own Hugging Face namespace, credited by name
(who).

cross_cutting.title: This week's local AI releases deserve a procurement test
cross_cutting.description: Meituan's November 10 announcement says LongCat-2.5 ... In its November 12 release, Edge0 reports that Edge0-145B reaches more than 80 decoding tokens per second with 29GB peak memory on a compatible laptop.
cross_cutting.content:
## DEV Community

A model license, a laptop performance claim and an inference-library release answer different questions. Treating them as one breakthrough is tempting. Treating them as separate checks is more useful for a company deciding whether to run AI on hardware it controls.

This week supplied an example of each. Meituan announced an MIT-licensed multimodal model. Edge0 reported a large model running on a compatible laptop. The llama.cpp maintainers released version 1.0.0 and explained how they will signal interface changes. Together, these are reasons to investigate local deployment, not proof that it will beat a hosted service for a particular business.

Start with permission. Meituan's November 10 announcement says LongCat-2.5 is available under the MIT license for commercial inference deployment and further training without extra authorization. Its published license permits use, modification and redistribution, subject to retaining the copyright and permission notice. That is a concrete input to a procurement review. It is not a service-level agreement: the same license provides the software "as is," without warranty.

Meituan describes LongCat-2.5 as a mixture-of-experts model with 1.6 trillion total parameters and about 48 billion activated per token, designed for long-running multimodal tasks. Those two parameter counts should not be confused. Activating fewer parameters for each token does not make the rest of the model disappear from the deployment plan. A buyer still needs a supported serving setup and a measured hardware budget. Nor should access to weights be confused with access to every ingredient of training.

Next comes fit. In its November 12 release, Edge0 reports that Edge0-145B reaches more than 80 decoding tokens per second with 29GB peak memory on a compatible laptop. These are company measurements, not an independent guarantee. Its comparison discusses a 48GB laptop, and the post also describes system-memory and SSD tiers. A headline memory number alone is therefore not a complete shopping specification. The company says the full hardware environment and reproduction instructions are being released with its technical report. Procurement should ask for those details and repeat the test on the intended machine, with realistic input lengths and concurrent applications.

Finally, consider maintenance. The llama.cpp team's November 13 post explains why version 1.0.0 matters to downstream developers: major-version bumps will signal public interface incompatibilities. The release notes also list server hardening and memory-management changes. That is useful engineering information, not a certification that an application is secure. A team embedding the library still needs an update owner, regression tests and a plan for breaking changes.

My recommendation is to turn these announcements into a small, bounded comparison. Choose one internal workload with clear acceptance criteria. Run the local candidate and the hosted alternative on the same permitted inputs. Measure output quality, response time, failures and the work needed to operate each option. Include hardware, electricity, maintenance and support in the cost estimate, rather than comparing a download price with an API invoice.

Give data handling its own test. Local inference can keep model inputs on controlled hardware, but an application may still call search, telemetry, storage or other online services. Inspect those connections before promising that nothing leaves the building. License freedom and network isolation are separate properties.

The purchasing question is not whether open models have won. It is whether a particular deployment meets the business's quality, cost and control requirements. This week's releases offer new candidates and useful infrastructure commitments. The next evidence should come from the buyer's own test, not a larger parameter count or a more confident launch headline.

## Sources

- Meituan, LongCat-2.5 open-source announcement (November 10, 2026): https://tech.meituan.com/2026/11/10/Meituan-LongCat-2.5-Open-Source.html
- Meituan, LongCat-2.5 model card: https://huggingface.co/meituan-longcat/LongCat-2.5
- Meituan, MIT license text: https://huggingface.co/meituan-longcat/LongCat-2.5/raw/main/LICENSE
- Edge0, Edge0-145B release (November 12, 2026): https://edge0.ai/blog/introducing-edge0-145b-frontier-ai-capabilities-on-your-own-computer
- ggml-org, llama.cpp v1.0.0 announcement (November 13, 2026): https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/llama-cpp-v1
- ggml-org, llama.cpp v1.0.0 release notes: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/tag/v1.0.0

# Grok Bot reportedly went from code to launch in seven weeks. Humans still get the veto.

Its builders describe Slack-based development and bots with ad budgets, but permissions and product decisions still need human judgment.

## TLDR

Grok Bot reportedly went from first code to launch in seven weeks. Lauren Tan says she built a feature with colleagues and bots in a 200-message Slack thread, using a Cursor cloud agent. She credits codebase guardrails for making that workflow possible. Roman Ugarte advocates expanding access gradually and says the team’s bottleneck is shifting toward product decisions. Producing more code isn’t permission to ship all of it.

Grok Bot, a tool for creating AI teammates, went from its first line of code to launch in seven weeks, according to Y Combinator. In a Lightcone episode uploaded November 14, 2026, core-team members Lauren Tan and Roman Ugarte describe their day-to-day workflows: bots working in Slack, coding agents checking their own output, and humans deciding which ideas deserve to become features. Source Source

Ugarte describes building an internal prototype in about seven weeks, releasing it internally and then bringing it to market. Neither account gives exact dates for those milestones. Source Source

The builders describe Grok Bot as a way to create AI teammates with names, identities and access to work tools, designed to work without waiting for each new prompt. Ugarte says their performance-marketing team gave a bot its own login, access to Google Ads and Facebook Ads, and a budget, with instructions to coordinate with a design bot on assets for A/B testing. He doesn’t provide the budget amount or campaign results. The coworker pitch has reached the expense-account stage. Source

## One Slack thread, not one magic prompt

Tan says she built an entire feature with her colleague Samantha, another product manager and her bot in a single Slack thread, without opening Cursor herself. That thread contained 200 messages. “One thread” is doing a lot of work there. Source

Cursor technology was still involved: Tan says her bot spawned a Cursor cloud agent, which could run the application and return prototype videos and screenshots. Keeping the discussion in a shared channel, she explains, let colleagues contribute feedback as the work developed, rather than waiting for her to return with a finished implementation. Source

Reaching that point required investment in agent instructions, codebase constraints and automated code checks, Tan says. She now lets agents merge their own pull requests—proposed code changes—and says she didn’t read the pull request for that particular feature, instead assessing the resulting software. Source

Tan recommends having agents run applications and examine results so they can find and fix problems. But she cautions that the loop doesn’t guarantee good code: a working implementation can still be slow or inefficient. For critical infrastructure, databases and deployment, she says engineers may still want to remain in the loop. Source

## Who gets access, and what gets shipped?

Ugarte advocates a gradual approach to permissions: start with limited, read-only work, assess the results and expand access as trust develops. He says there is no industry-wide silver-bullet answer to the permission problem, and describes bots owning whole job responsibilities as something still quite far away. A bot getting an ad budget isn’t an argument for handing it every password. Source

The team’s emerging bottleneck, in his account, is agreeing on the product roadmap. Ugarte describes discussions in which someone already has a proposed change built—but merging every available idea would leave the product without a coherent vision. For changes to the core interface, he says the team tests them internally and won’t ship them without clear internal support. Source

Tan cautions, “even though you can go really fast, it doesn't mean that you should just ship every feature you can think of.” She says her automated coding workflows focus more on maintenance, performance and bug fixes than feature development. Source

# Meta’s Muse: How we launched the most successful consumer product this year | Mona Sarantakos

DATE November 15, 2026SOURCE LENNY'SPARTICIPANTS LENNY RACHITSKY, MONA SARANTAKOS

// KEY TAKEAWAYS6 ITEMS

- 01Trust as the gating factor: 7 months of red-teaming before launch
- 02The origin was a "ping," not a roadmap: a weekend with OpenClaw on a Raspberry Pi
- 03A founder-mode build inside a giant company: prototype in hand, tiny team, no slide reviews
- 04Each leader had a distinct, specific imprint on the product
- 05Prototype-first PM: the role shifted from writing docs to taste and empathy
- 06Agent swarms as the new user research and eval-data engine

DAILY DIGEST · FREE · 06:00 ET

Like this? Get tomorrow's 7 best reads, distilled — 30 seconds each.

One click unsubscribe

## 1. Key Themes

### Trust as the gating factor: 7 months of red-teaming before launch

While OpenClaw-style competitors shipped in a couple of months, the Muse team deliberately spent roughly seven months, mostly on reliability, safety, and security, because a personal agent holds your email, calendar, and payment ability. Mona frames this as an existential, not a polish, decision. "There's a saying that we have internally, trust is a must. But really, like we were like in that, you know, it's like if we launch too early, and we have an issue like we have a bunch of issues, like that's it, right? People will not trust this agent, and if you don't trust the agent, you're never going to use it." 00:12:05. She also notes the team had to invent its own eval bar: "the benchmarks that are out in the industry just didn't feel sufficient to where we wanted to be for a product that's this I mean, it's got your personal context, right? Like it can go out and buy things for you." 00:11:37. Every new feature widened the attack surface: "in the very beginning, Muse didn't have a browser, right?... when you have a browser, suddenly you have a whole new set of problems that you have to solve, you know, from a security angle." 00:12:05. Her payoff: "we've like we, so far, haven't had a catastrophic problem." 00:13:21

### The origin was a "ping," not a roadmap: a weekend with OpenClaw on a Raspberry Pi

Muse was never a formally pitched project. Nat Friedman messaged a few people to try OpenClaw, and Mona's weekend experiment became the conviction. She had written in an H1 brief that consumer agents were an "end of 2026, maybe 2027" topic. Then: "I'm using OpenClaw. You guys need to get on it." (Nat Friedman, relayed by Mona) 00:03:41. The trigger moment was a Monday-morning school-newsletter digest: "it felt pretty magical and with such little direction from me... the idea that I could kind of suddenly feel really productive and on top of my shit, which I never felt on a Monday morning... was like incredible for me." 00:05:27. The team then self-selected: "It wasn't really a pitch as much as it was like a ping that just ended up consuming me completely... there wasn't even like a work stream." 00:06:32

### A founder-mode build inside a giant company: prototype in hand, tiny team, no slide reviews

Mona says this felt like her startup days, not Meta: "I've never experienced a product build like this before." 00:00:06. Leadership engaged through concrete artifacts instead of reviews: "We didn't do formal reviews, right? Like I didn't make any slides... we would give Mark our phone, be like, 'What do you think?' and he'd play around with it and give us feedback." 00:16:58. The core team started at roughly 10 people and stayed "under 100, all in, with all the functions," with only four PMs. "We were kind of obsessive over it... communication management and decision-making had to be very, very tight." 01:15:09

### Each leader had a distinct, specific imprint on the product

Nat was "an engineer's engineer" who helped design the Sentinel security backstop. Alex Wang's Muse Spark model "was way more agentic than we thought it was going to be," and he "pushed us out the door." Mark reframed the product's purpose. Mona on Mark: "The purpose of Muse is to make people's lives better and to help them achieve their goals." 00:20:44. That moved the team off task completion toward alignment with user priorities, which spawned "dreaming and studying" (background reasoning by the 24/7 agent) and the Goals tab. Mona: "once he kind of like opened that door, it was like you could see the engineers' eyes light up." 00:21:44

### Prototype-first PM: the role shifted from writing docs to taste and empathy

Mona argues that when anyone can prototype, the abstract-debate phase collapses: "we spend a lot more time discussing things in a concrete way versus an abstract way, right? Because it's like it's in my hands... I think that makes us move a lot faster than before." 01:02:19. The new differentiator is product taste: "the bar for PM has really changed. So like, product taste now is the most important thing... it's so easy to build shit and deploy shit, right? Like, AI slop is very easy to put out into the world." 01:02:19. It's also her top interview criterion.

### Agent swarms as the new user research and eval-data engine

Because Muse conversations are long-running and multi-turn, the team had no production data that looked like their use case. They sent agent swarms to mine conversations and generate synthetic data: "they were able to kind of like look at all of the conversations that are happening and data that's happening, and basically like kind of come back with... basically feed into our evals." 00:38:20. The key distinction from dashboards: "they're bringing back not just numbers, but insights, it creates a lot of empathy for what the users are going through... if you don't have that empathy and you can't feel the pain, you will never develop good products." 00:41:17. She now makes all her PMs use them.

### Use cases surprised the team: shopping exploded, home automation fizzled

Mona predicted personal productivity, health, and finance. "I did not think shopping was going to be as big of a use case as it's become." 00:32:04. Dogfooders drove it, and the team rebuilt evals around it. "Home automation, which we thought was going to be huge, just wasn't as big... it was like really big during the OpenClaw days, and I think partly because all the people who were using it probably also have a lot of home automation." 00:32:31. Early-adopter use cases did not predict mainstream ones. "Now shopping is one of our top use cases." 00:32:31

### Activation is the number one problem, and word of mouth beats advertising

"This is the number one problem that we have. People are like, 'Why? I already have a chatbot.'" 00:47:21. The most effective lever is seeing a peer use it: a mom passed her phone around and "two people downloaded it right there... no matter how much advertising we did... it didn't quite resonate until they saw somebody else that they related to using it." 00:47:21. Secondary levers: solving the frozen first prompt via an Ideas Tab of "starter packs," and tiered onboarding, since "what worked for the first cohort of users, which was like the early adopters, isn't going to work for later adopters." 00:47:21

### Personal-agent design: chat bubbles, one main chat, and an avatar you own

Muse deliberately rejected the industry's canvas/essay UI for chat bubbles, so it feels "like a messaging service... some sort of pattern that feels familiar to people about communicating with a human or an entity." 00:51:19. It chose a single main chat on the theory that "a personal assistant just has the memory of what happened before and everything happens in the same place." The internal fight was intense ("Team Main Chat, Team Side Chat"), and side chats were eventually added. The product principle underneath: "Muse is yours and... not like a Meta entity necessarily." 00:25:47

### The vision: ambient, democratized, proactive, and financially empowering

"Right now it's sort of trapped in an app, um, but I think soon it should be in your glasses, on your Charm devices, whatever that might be." 00:01:06. Beyond form factor, she wants less "babysitting" ("It's like a Tamagotchi") and a push toward economic betterment: "there's like a real opportunity for agents to be able to expand your world in lots of ways, including financial betterment." 01:21:09

## 2. Contrarian Perspectives

### Launching late was the right call in a race to ship

The industry rewarded speed. Lenny noted competitors shipped in a couple of months while Muse took seven. Mona, even when her husband asked if she regrets it: "I don't think I'd change anything. Like I really think that we like there was a bar we needed to hit. It took us the time that we needed to get there. And I'm glad that we did because... we, so far, haven't had a catastrophic problem." 00:12:46. In consumer agents, a first-mover advantage is worth less than the trust cost of an early security incident.

### Keep the quirky mascot and kill the corporate logo

Every few months someone said a stuffed-animal avatar couldn't ship from Meta. Mona's counter: "when you're talking to something that feels so personal, the last thing you want to talk to is a corporate logo, right? Like that breaks the spell completely." 00:00:50. Her broader thesis is that the agent's owner is the user and the parent brand should recede: "Meta kind of needs to fade away from that." 00:28:44. The "temporary" prototype creature became "a celebrity" and ad-campaign icon.

# Sri Lanka and Kazakhstan Discuss Cooperation on AI and Digital Infrastructure

Bilateral discussions between Sri Lanka and a delegation from Kazakhstan on AI data centres, Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) and AI governance were held on November 13 at the Ministry of Digital Economy, under the patronage of Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Engineer Ruwan Weeraratne.

The discussions focused on Kazakhstan’s experience in developing its national AI data centre, ensuring data sovereignty and integrating digital public services through platforms such as Smart Bridge, National Data Exchange (NDX) and SuperApp.

The two sides also exchanged knowledge on AI-based government services, including e-Gov GPT and the local language model KazLLM.

The discussions aimed to strengthen Sri Lanka’s national AI infrastructure and digital economy through international cooperation.

Dr. Hans Wijesuriya, Senior Advisor to the President on Digital Economy and Chairman of GovTech, and a Kazakhstan delegation led by Assem Kappar also attended the meeting.

cross_cutting.content:
# Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN, Infra Ink SAR2.5 Billion Worth of Agreements to Boost AI Infrastructure in the Kingdom

## The facilities mark the first transactions under the AI Data Center Financing Program by the National Infrastructure Fund (Infra).

By Inc.Arabia Staff

The Saudi government-backed development finance institution National Infrastructure Fund (Infra) and HUMAIN, the Public Investment Fund (PIF)-backed artificial intelligence (AI) firm, have penned two financing agreements worth up to SAR2.5 billion (US$667 million) to support computing deployment and power infrastructure for AI data centers in the Kingdom.

Under the agreements, a facility of up to SAR1.1 billion ($293.3 million) will fund the purchase and deployment of graphics processing units (GPUs), representing approximately 25 megawatts (MW) of information technology (IT) load. The second facility, worth up to SAR1.4 billion ($373.3 million), will finance substations, transmission infrastructure, and grid connections for HUMAIN’s AI data centers in the Kingdom. The planned infrastructure is designed to support future data center development with up to one gigawatt (GW) of IT capacity and help create conditions for investment by developers, hyperscalers, and institutional investors.

In a statement, Esmail bin Mohammed Alsallom, CEO of Infra, said: “Through these agreements, we aim to unlock investment well beyond Infra’s own commitment. Supporting HUMAIN’s computing deployment alongside essential power infrastructure helps prepare a broader pipeline of data center projects for investment. Our role is to strengthen project readiness and bankability, with commercial viability and economic value guiding how we deploy our capital. This partnership connects our priorities with commercial discipline, helping build a financing market that can attract a broader pool of private and institutional capital and sustain the local AI infrastructure growth.”

Tareq Amin, CEO of HUMAIN, added, “AI infrastructure is becoming foundational to the next generation of computing, and scaling it requires both significant investment and the infrastructure to support it. These facilities with Infra will help accelerate the deployment of advanced computing capacity and the power infrastructure required to support it. At HUMAIN, we are focused on building and operating AI infrastructure at scale, while developing the technologies and platforms that enable organizations and customers globally to put AI to work.”

The new facilities mark the first transactions under Infra’s AI Data Center Financing Program and build on a strategic framework announced by Infra and HUMAIN at Davos in January 2026, which outlined non-binding financing terms of up to SAR4.5 billion ($1.2 billion) for AI and digital infrastructure projects in Saudi Arabia.

Pictured in the lead image is a scene from the deal signing ceremony between Infra and HUMAIN.

cross_cutting.content:
# International partnerships offer developing economies a path to stronger AI capabilities

International partnerships are increasingly vital for developing economies seeking to strengthen their artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities. Recent cooperation initiatives highlight growing efforts to build domestic technological capacity while maintaining control over data, infrastructure and economic benefits.

Singapore, Ireland and Germany have recently advanced separate AI cooperation initiatives involving technology companies and international partners, reflecting a broader shift towards developing sovereign AI capabilities through collaboration rather than technological isolation.

Singapore's Ministry of Digital Development and Information signed a memorandum of understanding with Anthropic on October 14, covering AI safety, model evaluation and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.

That same day, Ireland secured support from participating European Union member states for the Dublin Declaration on Trusted, Safe and Sovereign Artificial Intelligence. The declaration calls for cooperation on digital infrastructure, workforce skills and strategic technological capacity.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and two federal ministries signed a joint declaration of intent with NVIDIA on October 19 to develop industrial AI models, although no timeline or budget has yet been disclosed.

Speaking at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, Merz described cooperation with NVIDIA as important for Germany's future success, highlighting AI's role in economic growth and industrial modernisation.

In Dublin, Ireland's Minister of State for Trade Promotion, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation, Niamh Smyth, described the declaration as "a strong political signal" of member states' commitment to accelerating work already under way at the European level.

These developments come amid growing international attention to the concentration of AI infrastructure and the need to expand technological capabilities across more countries.

A 2025 University of Oxford study found that only 32 countries host specialised AI data centres, while more than 150 countries have none. US and Chinese companies operate over 90% of the data centres used for AI-related work.

For developing economies, this concentration highlights the importance of international cooperation in gaining access to computing infrastructure, technical expertise and opportunities for domestic AI development.

In July, 29 countries, including Pakistan, Indonesia and Kazakhstan, became founding members of the Shanghai-based World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO).

Pakistan said its participation in the organisation would help narrow the global AI divide and strengthen international cooperation in emerging technologies.

The country approved its National AI Policy in 2025, and in February 2026, committed $1 billion by 2030 towards sovereign computing infrastructure and research, reflecting its efforts to develop domestic technological capabilities.

Experts believe such partnerships could help developing countries accelerate AI adoption, provided the agreements support local skills, technological independence and long-term economic value.

Dr Rachel Adams, Research Professor and Executive Director of the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence at the University of Cambridge and founding CEO of the Global Center on AI Governance, told Wealth Pakistan that the terms of AI partnerships were as important as the location of the technology itself.

"Hosting AI in your own country does not necessarily give you control if a foreign company still sets the prices, controls the technology, determines what you can do with it, and accumulates the value produced from it," she said.

Adams explained that for countries across the Global Majority, the real test was whether international agreements helped develop local skills and retain economic value.

She emphasised the importance of governments maintaining control over their people's data, preserving the ability to change technology suppliers and ensuring that AI systems could be directed towards locally defined development needs.

Hamza Ali Chaudhry, Executive Director of the Indus Institute for AI & Digital Policy and Founder and CEO of Poiesis AI Labs, told Wealth Pakistan that sovereign AI was increasingly becoming a matter of economic and national security.

However, he explained that technological sovereignty did not necessarily require countries to develop every component of AI infrastructure and technology independently.

Instead, developing economies needed sufficient domestic capacity to make informed technological choices, negotiate effective partnerships and pursue their own economic priorities.

Chaudhry said Pakistan's National AI Policy provided a foundation for developing such capabilities, but the next challenge was effective implementation.

He stressed the need to connect the policy with domestic research, computing infrastructure, data governance and commercial opportunities in sectors where AI could address local requirements.

These included AI applications for Urdu and regional languages, agriculture, healthcare and public services, where locally developed solutions could support economic and social development.

Chaudhry added that Pakistan's participation in WAICO should help strengthen these capabilities and attract meaningful international partnerships.

"Pakistan should not just adopt AI developed elsewhere; it should also have a stake in developing it and shaping the policies around it," he said.

The growing emphasis on sovereign AI partnerships suggests that countries are increasingly seeking technological capacity through international cooperation rather than pursuing complete self-reliance.

For developing economies such as Pakistan, the potential benefits extend beyond access to advanced AI systems to opportunities for research collaboration, workforce development, technology transfer and locally relevant applications.

However, experts emphasise that the long-term value of these partnerships will depend on whether participating countries retain meaningful control over their data, develop domestic expertise and secure a share of the economic benefits generated by AI.

Well-structured cooperation could therefore help developing countries move beyond adopting technologies developed elsewhere towards building the capacity to develop, adapt and shape AI systems according to their own economic and development priorities.

# Rackspace and Together AI sign inference infrastructure agreement

Rackspace and Together AI announced an infrastructure agreement, with deployment planned for 2027 subject to financing and other conditions.

Published 15 Nov 2026· 2 minute read

Rackspace and Together AI announced an initial multiyear inference infrastructure agreement on November 10, 2026. The agreement is binding, but deployment is planned for 2027 subject to conditions. It does not establish general availability of a new research service.

## A definitive agreement with conditional deployment

In its announcement, Rackspace says it expects to operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, including power, liquid cooling, networking and storage. Together AI expects to provide the managed platform. GPU financing had not been finalized; facilities, power and equipment availability are also conditions.

## The separate sales LOI is nonbinding

The companies also entered a nonbinding letter of intent to explore joint enterprise offerings. Those need further agreement. Data residency, security and compliance features would depend on the specific offering and customer arrangement.

## What universities need to establish in a service arrangement

For research offices assessing a future offering, our reading is that the service arrangement needs to specify data flows and operational responsibilities. Dedicated hardware alone does not answer where prompts, outputs and logs will go or who can use them. That assessment belongs alongside the institution’s research data governance review.

Together AI’s existing privacy documentation illustrates why separate questions matter: prompt storage is on by default, while sharing data for model training is a separate opt-in that is off by default. Its organization settings govern requests made with that organization’s API keys. These documented settings are context for evaluating a service, not confirmation of a future Rackspace configuration.

The zero data retention documentation also distinguishes request content from other records. Enabling the option affects subsequent requests; usage metadata remains, and explicitly uploaded fine-tuning or batch files remain stored until deleted. A university should establish which settings, retained records and deletion arrangements apply to its proposed workload.

NIST’s AI RMF Govern playbook recommends connecting AI risk management to data governance, model testing, monitoring and incident response. Applying that approach here means identifying who approves the workload, who reviews model outputs and who handles operational incidents. The NIST framework for research institutions and an AI governance framework template provide further context for assigning those responsibilities. These are institutional review considerations, not compliance findings about the announced infrastructure.
